Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.

=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller's SPA Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Bottom line:** The package moves almost all risk onto the Buyer. Each concession looks modest alone, but together they create a structure where the Buyer has very little real recourse. Several items also contradict the Seller's own Disclosure Letter. The specific disclosures on Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses and DD-006 describe live, unresolved risks, while the cover update calls them "addressed", "adequate" or "not material".

## Preliminary point: "FINAL" and "market standard"

The cover note says the positions were "settled at principal level", are "FINAL" and are "not intended to be re-opened". It also calls the caps, baskets and knowledge qualifiers "widely accepted market terms". These are the Seller's advocacy, not facts we should rely on.

- **Check with your principals.** We hold no record of agreement. Please confirm with the Wattlebridge principals whether anything was actually agreed. If it was, we need the terms, because some items below (e.g. the debt-free treatment of Riverlark and the bonuses) may already be covered by the agreed price mechanics in our favour.
- **Not binding until signed.** Nothing is binding until the SPA is executed, so the mark-up should be prepared on the merits.
- **"Market" claims prove nothing.** Even within the Seller's stated ranges, the draft picks the Seller-favourable end on every axis. It then adds terms that are not market on any view: an uncapped knowledge qualifier, general data-room disclosure, and limitations applied to fraud, title and tax.

---

## A. Liability architecture

### 1. Cap of 20% / AUD 4.8m (cl 12.1)
- **Why it matters:** This is the top of the Seller's own range, which is reasonable in isolation. But the Seller wants the same cap to cover title, capacity, tax, IP and "all Claims of any nature" (items 4 and 5). It is therefore effectively a cap on everything.
- **Push back:**
  - Accept a general warranty cap of about 20–30% only if everything else is fixed. Or, if W&I insurance is being considered, structure the cap around the policy.
  - Carve the following out of the general cap:
    - fundamental warranties (title, capacity, solvency): cap at 100% of price;
    - tax warranties and the tax indemnity: 100% of price;
    - specific indemnities (Ironquay, DD-006, bonuses, Sandbar if needed);
    - covenants, completion and leakage/debt adjustments;
    - fraud, wilful misconduct and deliberate concealment: uncapped.

### 2. De minimis AUD 25,000 and basket AUD 250,000 "excess only" (cl 12.2)
- **Why it matters:** The basket is about 1.04% of price and is a deductible, not a tipping basket. The first AUD 250k of valid loss is permanently lost. Claims under AUD 25k vanish entirely, and they do not even count towards the basket.
- **Push back:**
  - A **tipping basket** (once reached, recover from the first dollar) at about 0.5% (≈AUD 120k).
  - De minimis of about AUD 10k.
  - Claims arising from the same or related facts should aggregate for de minimis purposes.
  - Sub-de-minimis claims should count towards the basket.
  - None of the thresholds should apply to fundamental, tax, specific indemnity or fraud claims.

### 3. Time limits: 18 months, applied to "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (cl 12.3/13)
- **Why it matters:** The default-to-all drafting is the trap. If any carve-out is missed, tax, title and indemnity claims all fall under 18 months. That is plainly inadequate for tax, given ATO amendment periods for companies and the open-ended position where fraud or evasion is involved. It is also inadequate for title.
- **Push back:**
  - 18–24 months for general warranties. Ideally make it at least two audit cycles post-Completion.
  - Tax: the relevant amendment period plus about 3–6 months (commonly drafted as 5–7 years).
  - Title and capacity: the statutory limitation period. Under the *Limitation Act 1969* (NSW) this is generally 6 years for contract and 12 years if the SPA is executed as a deed.
  - Specific indemnities: a bespoke period tied to the risk.
  - Reverse the default, so that limitations apply only to **General Warranty Claims** unless expressly extended.

### 4. Title and capacity warranties under the same cap and time limits
- **Why it matters:** "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason. If title fails, the Buyer has paid AUD 24m for shares it does not own, yet it could recover only AUD 4.8m, after a basket, within 18 months.
- **Push back:** Reject outright. Fundamental warranties should be capped at 100% of price (plus costs), carry the statutory limitation period, and sit outside the de minimis, basket and knowledge qualifier.

### 5. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applied to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5)
- **Why it matters:** As drafted, these could be argued to cap or exclude:
  - fraud claims;
  - claims for misleading or deceptive conduct (statutory protections cannot be fully excluded by contract, but the Seller will still rely on the clause);
  - specific indemnities;
  - breach of the pre-Completion conduct covenants;
  - the debt-free/cash-free price adjustment itself.
- **Push back:**
  - Express carve-outs for fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment, covenants, specific indemnities, completion and price adjustments, and leakage.
  - The non-reliance clause should exclude reliance only on statements *outside* the Warranties, the Disclosure Letter and the SPA. It must not cut back reliance on the Warranties themselves.
  - Preserve specific performance and termination rights.

---

## B. Disclosure and knowledge

### 6. General disclosure of the data room, Accounts, registers and public records (Disclosure Letter §1.1–1.2)
- **Why it matters:** This qualifies every warranty against thousands of documents. The Seller is effectively converting the warranties into "buyer beware". It also undermines W&I cover, because insurers exclude matters that are disclosed. The data room is fixed at 22 September 2026, now about six weeks old.
- **Push back:**
  - Only **specific** disclosures in the Disclosure Letter qualify the warranties, and only against the warranties they are expressly made against.
  - Each disclosure must be fair, meaning sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and assess its impact.
  - If some data-room disclosure has to be conceded, limit it to named documents, with the fair-disclosure standard still applying.
  - No general disclosure of "publicly searchable records" beyond a short, defined list of searches (e.g. ASIC, PPSR) as at a fixed date.
  - Any bring-down or updated disclosure before Completion must not cure a breach. It should only inform the Buyer's termination right.
- **§1.4 (non-admission):** Generally acceptable. But the SPA should make clear that §1.4 does not dilute the specific facts disclosed, which we are entitled to rely on as accurate.

### 7. Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3)
- **Why it matters:** This is the most dangerous single clause. It is an anti-sandbagging provision with three expansions:
  1. it covers the Buyer **and its advisers**;
  2. it covers anything **"discoverable"** (constructive knowledge), not just actual knowledge;
  3. it covers the entire data room and public records.

  Combined with general disclosure, almost every claim becomes defensible. It also contradicts the logic of a specific indemnity: we know about Ironquay and DD-006 precisely *because* they were disclosed.
- **Push back:**
  - Delete it and replace it with an express statement that Buyer knowledge (actual, constructive or imputed) does not affect any claim. Australian authority on this point is not entirely settled, so an express clause matters.
  - Fallback: limit the exclusion to the *actual* knowledge, as at signing, of a short list of named Wattlebridge deal-team individuals, of matters *fairly disclosed* in the Disclosure Letter. Exclude advisers. Exclude fundamental, tax and specific indemnity claims.

---

## C. Specific transaction risks

### 8. Bluefen change-control consent (cl 3/6.3; DD-002; DL §2)
- **Facts:**
  - Bluefen accounts for about AUD 3.6m, roughly 30% of FY26 revenue.
  - Its contract has a change-control consent clause (11.2) with conditions (11.3).
  - There is no consent, and no evidence that the conditions are satisfied.
- **Why it matters:** The cover update says this is "addressed". It is not. The proposed mechanism is "reasonable endeavours", deemed satisfied on delivery of *any* written consent. That would let a consent given on adverse conditions (repricing, a shorter term, new termination rights, a guarantee) satisfy the condition precedent. Losing or impairing 30% of revenue would go straight to valuation.
- **Push back:**
  - Make it a condition precedent: Bluefen's **unconditional** written consent, or consent on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably, with all clause 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived **in writing by Bluefen**.
  - No amendment to the Bluefen contract without Buyer consent.
  - The Seller must use **all reasonable endeavours**, with Buyer participation in communications and approval of the approach.
  - Buyer-only right to waive the condition.
  - A long-stop date with a Buyer termination right.
  - Consider a price adjustment, earn-out or retention if consent is late or conditional.
  - A warranty that no notice of termination, non-renewal or dispute has been received.

### 9. Riverlark facility (cl 2/7; DD-003; DL §3)
- **Facts:**
  - About AUD 3.2m is outstanding.
  - There is a change-of-control clause (8.1) and a discharge clause (9.2).
  - The facility is not repaid and no discharge has been obtained.
- **Why it matters:** A release "following Completion" means Completion itself probably triggers a default or event of review under clause 8.1. The Company would be left with an outstanding facility and security over its assets in the Buyer's hands. This is incompatible with the debt-free basis of the deal.
- **Push back:**
  - Treat the facility as Debt and repay it **at Completion** from the purchase price, directly to Riverlark under the funds flow.
  - Completion deliverables:
    - a signed payout letter confirming the exact payout figure as at Completion (including break costs and fees);
    - a deed of release;
    - an undertaking to lodge PPSR financing change statements (or the actual lodgements);
    - return of any title documents.
  - A covenant that no further drawdowns will be made before Completion.
  - Any shortfall is deducted from price.

### 10. DD-005 Completion bonuses of AUD 420,000 (funds flow; DL §5)
- **Why it matters:** "A matter for the Seller" sounds reassuring, but the **Company** is the employer. Once the Buyer owns it, the liability sits with the Company, plus payroll tax, possible superannuation, PAYG withholding and other on-costs. Leaving them out of the funds flow moves AUD 420k+ of value to the Buyer, contrary to the debt-free/cash-free basis.
- **Push back:**
  - Define the bonuses and all associated on-costs as Transaction Costs or Debt, deducted from price.
  - Pay them through payroll at or immediately after Completion, with the withheld amounts funded from the price.
  - A specific indemnity for any shortfall, outside the cap and basket.
  - Full particulars: recipients, conditions, any "good leaver" acceleration, and whether any amount is payable if an employee leaves after Completion.
  - A warranty that no other change-of-control or transaction payments exist.

### 11. Ironquay IP: SOW3 (cl 11.1; DD-004, DD-010; DL §4)
- **Facts:**
  - Ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials passes only on cleared payment of **every** SOW3 fee.
  - DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open.
  - There is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment.
- **Why it matters:** For a SaaS business, a gap in IP ownership goes to the core asset. The current indemnity covers only "the SOW3 payment", meaning the AUD 180k. It does not cover the real exposure: that the Company may not own code embedded in its product. That exposure includes:
  - infringement claims;
  - injunction risk;
  - rework costs;
  - customer claims.
- **Push back:**
  - Before Completion: proof of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees (or payment from price at Completion).
  - A confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay covering all SOW3 Project Materials, with moral rights consents from individual authors where relevant.
  - Make both a condition precedent or a Completion deliverable.
  - Broaden the indemnity to all Loss arising from the Company not owning, or not having unencumbered rights to, the SOW3 materials. This indemnity should sit outside the cap, basket and knowledge qualifier, with a long survival period.
  - Strengthen the IP warranties rather than "settling" them under the general regime.

### 12. DD-006 export/privacy incident (cl 4.6/Sch 6; DL §6)
- **Facts:**
  - A download link went to an unintended external address.
  - About 1,240 records were exposed: names, business emails, roles and timestamps.
  - Access, scope and notification obligations are all undetermined.
  - The investigation is described as preliminary as at 22 September 2026.
- **Why it matters:**
  - Business contact details are still personal information under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth).
  - If this is a suspected eligible data breach, the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme requires a reasonable and expeditious assessment, generally within 30 days. Given today's date, that period may already have run.
  - Late or missed notification is a regulatory exposure in its own right, separate from the underlying incident.
  - The Bluefen and other customer contracts may also impose their own breach-notice obligations.
  - "Not expected to be material" is an assertion the disclosed facts do not support.
- **Push back:**
  - Immediate information request: incident date, the assessment and its conclusions, any OAIC or individual notifications, any forensic report, link access logs, and customer notifications given.
  - A covenant to complete the assessment and comply with all notification obligations before Completion, in consultation with the Buyer.
  - A **specific indemnity** for all Loss arising from DD-006, including regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully indemnifiable, notification and remediation costs, customer claims and credits. It should sit outside the cap and basket, survive at least 3 years, and not be qualified by disclosure or knowledge.
  - Consider a retention or escrow amount.
  - Privacy and data warranties should be brought down to Completion.

### 13. Sandbar supplier renewals: 3 × AUD 110,000 = AUD 330,000 (DD-008/DD-011; DL §8)
- **Why it matters:**
  - The Disclosure Letter itself says the three renewals should be "read together for timing/scope". That is a strong hint they are one arrangement split into three.
  - Each amount may sit just under a material-contract, conduct-of-business or approval threshold. Check our SPA thresholds.
  - Calling them "ordinary course" is the Seller's characterisation. The Disclosure Letter expressly does **not** say whether they are unavoidable, terminable or accrued.
  - Splitting also helps the Seller under the de minimis and basket.
- **Push back:**
  - Obtain the contracts and dates. Were they signed after the economic or locked-box date, or without the approval the conduct covenants require?
  - Treat any prepaid, committed or unbudgeted amounts as Debt or leakage as appropriate.
  - Require termination for convenience if they are not needed.
  - Aggregate related contracts for all threshold purposes.
  - A specific indemnity if they turn out to be non-ordinary-course commitments.

### 14. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"
- **Push back:** Reject.
  - Tax needs a standalone tax indemnity or deed covering pre-Completion tax, with the tax amendment period as the limitation, recovery up to 100% of price, and no basket.
  - The deal conventions should also be agreed: conduct of tax claims, cooperation, and pre-Completion returns.
  - IP should be treated as a quasi-fundamental warranty given the SaaS asset, with a higher cap and longer survival period.

### 15. Title evidenced only by the share register at DD-012 (DL §10)
- **Why it matters:** The register is the Company's own record. DL §10 itself says the Buyer has not verified it.
- **Push back:**
  - A full title warranty (fundamental): legal and beneficial ownership of 100% of the issued shares, fully paid, free of Encumbrances, with no options, convertibles or rights to issue.
  - Verify independently through an ASIC company extract and the PPSR search against the Seller and the Company. Reconcile the issue history.
  - Completion deliverables:
    - executed share transfers;
    - share certificates (or an indemnity for lost certificates);
    - updated register;
    - director resignations;
    - releases of any Encumbrances over the shares.

### 16. Lower-priority items: Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
- **Lease:** The Disclosure Letter describes a notification obligation, not a consent requirement. Confirm against the lease itself (check any change-of-control definition and any bank guarantee). Add a covenant for the Seller or Company to give the notice in the required form and on time.
- **Mossvale:** The restriction is on *assignment*. Confirm there is no change-of-control or deemed-assignment definition elsewhere in the contract. If there is none, a confirmatory warranty is sufficient.

---

## D. Inconsistencies to put to Seller counsel

| Seller update says | Seller's own Disclosure Letter says |
|---|---|
| Bluefen consent "addressed" | No consent; conditions in 11.3 not shown satisfied (§2) |
| Riverlark released "following Completion" | Not repaid, no discharge, change-control clause 8.1 (§3) |
| Ironquay indemnity "adequate" | No payment receipt, no assignment, title depends on payment (§4) |
| Bonuses "a matter for the Seller" | Not in funds flow; on-costs unaddressed (§5) |
| DD-006 "not expected to be material" | Access, scope and notification all undetermined (§6) |
| Sandbar "ordinary course" | Letter expressly does not say so; flags reading the three together (§8) |

---

## E. Summary of recommendations

1. **Do not accept the "FINAL" framing.** Confirm internally what, if anything, was agreed at principal level, then issue a full mark-up.
2. **Restructure liability:**
   - general cap of about 20–30%, only with carve-outs;
   - fundamental and tax warranties at 100% of price;
   - fraud uncapped;
   - tipping basket of about 0.5% with aggregation;
   - de minimis of about AUD 10k;
   - general claims 18–24 months, tax for the amendment period plus a buffer, title for the statutory limitation period;
   - reverse the "applies to all Claims" default.
3. **Strike general disclosure.** Only specific, fair disclosure against identified warranties; bring-down disclosure must not cure breaches.
4. **Delete cl 8.3** and insert a pro-sandbagging clause. Fallback: actual knowledge of named individuals of fairly disclosed matters only.
5. **Carve fraud, covenants, specific indemnities and price adjustments** out of the limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses.
6. **Bluefen:** condition precedent requiring unconditional (or Buyer-acceptable) consent with 11.3 conditions satisfied, all reasonable endeavours, Buyer waiver only, long-stop and termination right; consider value protection.
7. **Riverlark:** repaid from price at Completion; payout letter, deed of release and PPSR discharges as Completion deliverables.
8. **Bonuses:** AUD 420k plus all on-costs treated as Debt or Transaction Costs, deducted from price and run through payroll; specific indemnity.
9. **Ironquay:** payment verified, confirmatory assignment as a condition precedent or deliverable, broad standalone IP indemnity.
10. **DD-006:** urgent information request; Seller covenant on NDB compliance; specific indemnity outside the cap and basket; consider a retention.
11. **Sandbar:** get the contracts, test them against the conduct covenants and thresholds, treat committed amounts as Debt or leakage, aggregate for thresholds.
12. **Tax and IP:** standalone tax indemnity; IP as quasi-fundamental.
13. **Title:** fundamental warranty plus independent ASIC/PPSR verification and full Completion deliverables.
14. **Consider W&I insurance** to bridge the cap gap. Note that the Seller's general disclosure and knowledge terms would also undermine W&I cover, which is a further reason to resist them.
15. **Retention or escrow** (sized to the Bluefen, Ironquay and DD-006 exposures) as a backstop if the Seller's covenant strength is uncertain post-sale.

The suggested percentages and periods are opening negotiating positions, not statements of a fixed market standard. They should be calibrated with the deal team against the commercial priorities and any W&I quotes. If useful, I can turn this into a clause-by-clause mark-up schedule or a short issues list to send to Seller counsel.

  - Tax: the relevant amendment period plus about 3–6 months (commonly drafted as 5–7 years).
  - Title and capacity: the statutory limitation period. Under the *Limitation Act 1969* (NSW) this is generally 6 years for contract and 12 years if the SPA is executed as a deed.
  - Specific indemnities: a bespoke period tied to the risk.
  - Reverse the default, so that limitations apply only to **General Warranty Claims** unless expressly extended.

### 4. Title and capacity warranties under the same cap and time limits
- **Why it matters:** "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason. If title fails, the Buyer has paid AUD 24m for shares it does not own, yet it could recover only AUD 4.8m, after a basket, within 18 months.
- **Push back:** Reject outright. Fundamental warranties should be capped at 100% of price (plus costs), carry the statutory limitation period, and sit outside the de minimis, basket and knowledge qualifier.

### 5. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applied to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5)
- **Why it matters:** As drafted, these could be argued to cap or exclude:
  - fraud claims;
  - claims for misleading or deceptive conduct (statutory protections cannot be fully excluded by contract, but the Seller will still rely on the clause);
  - specific indemnities;
  - breach of the pre-Completion conduct covenants;
  - the debt-free/cash-free price adjustment itself.
- **Push back:**
  - Express carve-outs for fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment, covenants, specific indemnities, completion and price adjustments, and leakage.
  - The non-reliance clause should exclude reliance only on statements *outside* the Warranties, the Disclosure Letter and the SPA. It must not cut back reliance on the Warranties themselves.
  - Preserve specific performance and termination rights.

## B. Disclosure and knowledge

### 6. General disclosure of the data room, Accounts, registers and public records (Disclosure Letter §1.1–1.2)
- **Why it matters:** This qualifies every warranty against thousands of documents. The Seller is effectively converting the warranties into "buyer beware". It also undermines W&I cover, because insurers exclude matters that are disclosed. The data room is fixed at 22 September 2026, now about six weeks old.
- **Push back:**
  - Only **specific** disclosures in the Disclosure Letter qualify the warranties, and only against the warranties they are expressly made against.
  - Each disclosure must be fair, meaning sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and assess its impact.
  - If some data-room disclosure has to be conceded, limit it to named documents, with the fair-disclosure standard still applying.
  - No general disclosure of "publicly searchable records" beyond a short, defined list of searches (e.g. ASIC, PPSR) as at a fixed date.
  - Any bring-down or updated disclosure before Completion must not cure a breach. It should only inform the Buyer's termination right.
- **§1.4 (non-admission):** Generally acceptable. But the SPA should make clear that §1.4 does not dilute the specific facts disclosed, which we are entitled to rely on as accurate.

### 7. Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3)
- **Why it matters:** This is the most dangerous single clause. It is an anti-sandbagging provision with three expansions:
  1. it covers the Buyer **and its advisers**;
  2. it covers anything **"discoverable"** (constructive knowledge), not just actual knowledge;
  3. it covers the entire data room and public records.

  Combined with general disclosure, almost every claim becomes defensible. It also contradicts the logic of a specific indemnity: we know about Ironquay and DD-006 precisely *because* they were disclosed.
- **Push back:**
  - Delete it and replace it with an express statement that Buyer knowledge (actual, constructive or imputed) does not affect any claim. Australian authority on this point is not entirely settled, so an express clause matters.
  - Fallback: limit the exclusion to the *actual* knowledge, as at signing, of a short list of named Wattlebridge deal-team individuals, of matters *fairly disclosed* in the Disclosure Letter. Exclude advisers. Exclude fundamental, tax and specific indemnity claims.

## C. Specific transaction risks

### 8. Bluefen change-control consent (cl 3/6.3; DD-002; DL §2)
- **Facts:**
  - Bluefen accounts for about AUD 3.6m, roughly 30% of FY26 revenue.
  - Its contract has a change-control consent clause (11.2) with conditions (11.3).
  - There is no consent, and no evidence that the conditions are satisfied.
- **Why it matters:** The cover update says this is "addressed". It is not. The proposed mechanism is "reasonable endeavours", deemed satisfied on delivery of *any* written consent. That would let a consent given on adverse conditions (repricing, a shorter term, new termination rights, a guarantee) satisfy the condition precedent. Losing or impairing 30% of revenue would go straight to valuation.
- **Push back:**
  - Make it a condition precedent: Bluefen's **unconditional** written consent, or consent on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably, with all clause 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived **in writing by Bluefen**.
  - No amendment to the Bluefen contract without Buyer consent.
  - The Seller must use **all reasonable endeavours**, with Buyer participation in communications and approval of the approach.
  - Buyer-only right to waive the condition.
  - A long-stop date with a Buyer termination right.
  - Consider a price adjustment, earn-out or retention if consent is late or conditional.
  - A warranty that no notice of termination, non-renewal or dispute has been received.

### 9. Riverlark facility (cl 2/7; DD-003; DL §3)
- **Facts:**
  - About AUD 3.2m is outstanding.
  - There is a change-of-control clause (8.1) and a discharge clause (9.2).
  - The facility is not repaid and no discharge has been obtained.
- **Why it matters:** A release "following Completion" means Completion itself probably triggers a default or event of review under clause 8.1. The Company would be left with an outstanding facility and security over its assets in the Buyer's hands. This is incompatible with the debt-free basis of the deal.
- **Push back:**
  - Treat the facility as Debt and repay it **at Completion** from the purchase price, directly to Riverlark under the funds flow.
  - Completion deliverables:
    - a signed payout letter confirming the exact payout figure as at Completion (including break costs and fees);
    - a deed of release;
    - an undertaking to lodge PPSR financing change statements (or the actual lodgements);
    - return of any title documents.
  - A covenant that no further drawdowns will be made before Completion.
  - Any shortfall is deducted from price.

### 10. DD-005 Completion bonuses of AUD 420,000 (funds flow; DL §5)
- **Why it matters:** "A matter for the Seller" sounds reassuring, but the **Company** is the employer. Once the Buyer owns it, the liability sits with the Company, plus payroll tax, possible superannuation, PAYG withholding and other on-costs. Leaving them out of the funds flow moves AUD 420k+ of value to the Buyer, contrary to the debt-free/cash-free basis.
- **Push back:**
  - Define the bonuses and all associated on-costs as Transaction Costs or Debt, deducted from price.
  - Pay them through payroll at or immediately after Completion, with the withheld amounts funded from the price.
  - A specific indemnity for any shortfall, outside the cap and basket.
  - Full particulars: recipients, conditions, any "good leaver" acceleration, and whether any amount is payable if an employee leaves after Completion.
  - A warranty that no other change-of-control or transaction payments exist.

### 11. Ironquay IP: SOW3 (cl 11.1; DD-004, DD-010; DL §4)
- **Facts:**
  - Ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials passes only on cleared payment of **every** SOW3 fee.
  - DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open.
  - There is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment.
- **Why it matters:** For a SaaS business, a gap in IP ownership goes to the core asset. The current indemnity covers only "the SOW3 payment", meaning the AUD 180k. It does not cover the real exposure: that the Company may not own code embedded in its product. That exposure includes:
  - infringement claims;
  - injunction risk;
  - rework costs;
  - customer claims.
- **Push back:**
  - Before Completion: proof of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees (or payment from price at Completion).
  - A confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay covering all SOW3 Project Materials, with moral rights consents from individual authors where relevant.
  - Make both a condition precedent or a Completion deliverable.
  - Broaden the indemnity to all Loss arising from the Company not owning, or not having unencumbered rights to, the SOW3 materials. This indemnity should sit outside the cap, basket and knowledge qualifier, with a long survival period.
  - Strengthen the IP warranties rather than "settling" them under the general regime.

### 12. DD-006 export/privacy incident (cl 4.6/Sch 6; DL §6)
- **Facts:**
  - A download link went to an unintended external address.
  - About 1,240 records were exposed: names, business emails, roles and timestamps.
  - Access, scope and notification obligations are all undetermined.
  - The investigation is described as preliminary as at 22 September 2026.
- **Why it matters:**
  - Business contact details are still personal information under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth).
  - If this is a suspected eligible data breach, the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme requires a reasonable and expeditious assessment, generally within 30 days. Given today's date, that period may already have run.
  - Late or missed notification is a regulatory exposure in its own right, separate from the underlying incident.
  - The Bluefen and other customer contracts may also impose their own breach-notice obligations.
  - "Not expected to be material" is an assertion the disclosed facts do not support.
- **Push back:**
  - Immediate information request: incident date, the assessment and its conclusions, any OAIC or individual notifications, any forensic report, link access logs, and customer notifications given.
  - A covenant to complete the assessment and comply with all notification obligations before Completion, in consultation with the Buyer.
  - A **specific indemnity** for all Loss arising from DD-006, including regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully indemnifiable, notification and remediation costs, customer claims and credits. It should sit outside the cap and basket, survive at least 3 years, and not be qualified by disclosure or knowledge.
  - Consider a retention or escrow amount.
  - Privacy and data warranties should be brought down to Completion.

### 13. Sandbar supplier renewals: 3 × AUD 110,000 = AUD 330,000 (DD-008/DD-011; DL §8)
- **Why it matters:**
  - The Disclosure Letter itself says the three renewals should be "read together for timing/scope". That is a strong hint they are one arrangement split into three.
  - Each amount may sit just under a material-contract, conduct-of-business or approval threshold. Check our SPA thresholds.
  - Calling them "ordinary course" is the Seller's characterisation. The Disclosure Letter expressly does **not** say whether they are unavoidable, terminable or accrued.
  - Splitting also helps the Seller under the de minimis and basket.
- **Push back:**
  - Obtain the contracts and dates. Were they signed after the economic or locked-box date, or without the approval the conduct covenants require?
  - Treat any prepaid, committed or unbudgeted amounts as Debt or leakage as appropriate.
  - Require termination for convenience if they are not needed.
  - Aggregate related contracts for all threshold purposes.
  - A specific indemnity if they turn out to be non-ordinary-course commitments.

### 14. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"
- **Push back:** Reject.
  - Tax needs a standalone tax indemnity or deed covering pre-Completion tax, with the tax amendment period as the limitation, recovery up to 100% of price, and no basket.
  - The deal conventions should also be agreed: conduct of tax claims, cooperation, and pre-Completion returns.
  - IP should be treated as a quasi-fundamental warranty given the SaaS asset, with a higher cap and longer survival period.

### 15. Title evidenced only by the share register at DD-012 (DL §10)
- **Why it matters:** The register is the Company's own record. DL §10 itself says the Buyer has not verified it.
- **Push back:**
  - A full title warranty (fundamental): legal and beneficial ownership of 100% of the issued shares, fully paid, free of Encumbrances, with no options, convertibles or rights to issue.
  - Verify independently through an ASIC company extract and the PPSR search against the Seller and the Company. Reconcile the issue history.
  - Completion deliverables:
    - executed share transfers;
    - share certificates (or an indemnity for lost certificates);
    - updated register;
    - director resignations;
    - releases of any Encumbrances over the shares.

### 16. Lower-priority items: Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
- **Lease:** The Disclosure Letter describes a notification obligation, not a consent requirement. Confirm against the lease itself (check any change-of-control definition and any bank guarantee). Add a covenant for the Seller or Company to give the notice in the required form and on time.
- **Mossvale:** The restriction is on *assignment*. Confirm there is no change-of-control or deemed-assignment definition elsewhere in the contract. If there is none, a confirmatory warranty is sufficient.

## E. Summary of recommendations

1. **Do not accept the "FINAL" framing.** Confirm internally what, if anything, was agreed at principal level, then issue a full mark-up.
2. **Restructure liability:**
   - general cap of about 20–30%, only with carve-outs;
   - fundamental and tax warranties at 100% of price;
   - fraud uncapped;
   - tipping basket of about 0.5% with aggregation;
   - de minimis of about AUD 10k;
   - general claims 18–24 months, tax for the amendment period plus a buffer, title for the statutory limitation period;
   - reverse the "applies to all Claims" default.
3. **Strike general disclosure.** Only specific, fair disclosure against identified warranties; bring-down disclosure must not cure breaches.
4. **Delete cl 8.3** and insert a pro-sandbagging clause. Fallback: actual knowledge of named individuals of fairly disclosed matters only.
5. **Carve fraud, covenants, specific indemnities and price adjustments** out of the limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses.
6. **Bluefen:** condition precedent requiring unconditional (or Buyer-acceptable) consent with 11.3 conditions satisfied, all reasonable endeavours, Buyer waiver only, long-stop and termination right; consider value protection.
7. **Riverlark:** repaid from price at Completion; payout letter, deed of release and PPSR discharges as Completion deliverables.
8. **Bonuses:** AUD 420k plus all on-costs treated as Debt or Transaction Costs, deducted from price and run through payroll; specific indemnity.
9. **Ironquay:** payment verified, confirmatory assignment as a condition precedent or deliverable, broad standalone IP indemnity.
10. **DD-006:** urgent information request; Seller covenant on NDB compliance; specific indemnity outside the cap and basket; consider a retention.
11. **Sandbar:** get the contracts, test them against the conduct covenants and thresholds, treat committed amounts as Debt or leakage, aggregate for thresholds.
12. **Tax and IP:** standalone tax indemnity; IP as quasi-fundamental.
13. **Title:** fundamental warranty plus independent ASIC/PPSR verification and full Completion deliverables.
14. **Consider W&I insurance** to bridge the cap gap. Note that the Seller's general disclosure and knowledge terms would also undermine W&I cover, which is a further reason to resist them.
15. **Retention or escrow** (sized to the Bluefen, Ironquay and DD-006 exposures) as a backstop if the Seller's covenant strength is uncertain post-sale.

The suggested percentages and periods are opening negotiating positions, not statements of a fixed market standard. They should be calibrated with the deal team against the commercial priorities and any W&I quotes. If useful, I can turn this into a clause-by-clause mark-up schedule or a short issues list to send to Seller counsel.
